chmmc-2012-winter-power-01.title: Pythagoras
chmmc-2012-winter-power-01.body:
Two circles of radii $r_1,r_2$ tangent to each other and to the $x$-axis have tangency points at horizontal distance $\sqrt{(r_1+r_2)^2-(r_1-r_2)^2}=2\sqrt{r_1r_2}$. Figure 1: the new circle has radius $r$ and touches the unit circles (radius $\frac12$), so by symmetry its tangency point is $\left(\frac12,0\right)$ at horizontal distance $2\sqrt{r/2}=\frac12$ from $(0,0)$, giving $r=\frac18$, diameter $\frac14$. Figure 2: it lies between the unit circle at $(0,0)$ (radius $\frac12$) and the circle of radius $\frac18$ centered above $(\frac12,0)$. If its radius is $s$ and tangency point $(t,0)$: $t=2\sqrt{s/2}=\sqrt{2s}$ and $\frac12-t=2\sqrt{s/8}=\sqrt{s/2}$, so $\sqrt{s/2}\,(2+1)=\frac12$, $\sqrt{s/2}=\frac16$, $s=\frac1{18}$ and $t=\frac13$. The diameter is $\frac19$.

**Answer: diameters $\frac14$ and $\frac19$; points $(\frac12,0)$ and $(\frac13,0)$**

chmmc-2012-winter-power-02.title: Horizontal distances
chmmc-2012-winter-power-02.body:
Tangent circles of radii $r_1,r_2$ that both touch the $x$-axis have their axis-touching points $2\sqrt{r_1r_2}$ apart (right triangle with legs $|r_1-r_2|$ and the horizontal distance, hypotenuse $r_1+r_2$). Let the radii be $x=\frac{a^2}2$, $y=\frac{b^2}2$, $z$. Then $XY=2\sqrt{xy}$, $XZ=2\sqrt{xz}$, $ZY=2\sqrt{yz}$. $C_3$ sits in the gap under the contact point of $C_1,C_2$, so $Z$ lies between $X$ and $Y$ and $XZ+ZY=XY$: $\sqrt z(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)=\sqrt{xy}$, hence $z=\frac{xy}{(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)^2}=\frac{a^2b^2}{2(a+b)^2}$ and the diameter is $2z=\frac{a^2b^2}{(a+b)^2}$. Also $\frac{XZ}{ZY}=\sqrt{\frac xy}=\frac ab$.

**Answer: diameter $\frac{a^2b^2}{(a+b)^2}$, ratio $\frac ab$**

chmmc-2012-winter-power-03.title: Distance formula
chmmc-2012-winter-power-03.body: Both circles lie above the $x$-axis and touch it at different points, so they can only be tangent externally (an internally tangent smaller circle would touch the axis at the same point as the larger one). The centres are $\left(\frac ab,\frac1{2b^2}\right)$ and $\left(\frac cd,\frac1{2d^2}\right)$, so the circles are tangent iff $$\left(\frac1{2b^2}+\frac1{2d^2}\right)^2=\left(\frac ab-\frac cd\right)^2+\left(\frac1{2b^2}-\frac1{2d^2}\right)^2.$$ Moving the last term and using the difference of squares, $\frac1{b^2d^2}=\left(\frac ab-\frac cd\right)^2=\frac{(ad-bc)^2}{b^2d^2}$, i.e. $(ad-bc)^2=1$. Every step is reversible. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-04.title: Bezout
chmmc-2012-winter-power-04.body: Since $\gcd(p,q)=1$ there are integers $x,y$ with $px+qy=1$. Put $a=kp+y$, $b=kq-x$ and choose $k$ with $0<a\le p$. Then $aq-bp=yq+xp=1$. Let $c=p-a$, $d=q-b$; then $a+c=p$, $b+d=q$ and $cq-dp=pq-aq-qp+bp=-(aq-bp)=-1$, so $|cq-dp|=1$ (this also shows both fractions are in lowest terms). It remains to show $0<a\le b$ and $0\le c<d$. By construction $0<a\le p$, so $0\le c<p$. From $bp=aq-1$ and $q>p$: $b=\frac{aq-1}p\ge\frac{q(a-1)}p>a-1$, so $b\ge a$. Likewise $d=\frac{cq+1}p>\frac{cq}p\ge c$ (using $q>p$ and $c\ge0$). So $0<\frac ab\le1$ and $0\le\frac cd<1$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-05a.title: Induction
chmmc-2012-winter-power-05a.body: Claim (extended to $0\le\frac pq\le1$): the configuration contains the circle of diameter $\frac1{q^2}$ tangent at $\left(\frac pq,0\right)$. For $q=1$ these are the two starting circles. Let $q\ge2$ and assume the claim for all denominators $<q$. Take $\frac ab,\frac cd$ from (iii); $b,d\ge1$ and $b+d=q$, so $b,d<q$. By induction the circles $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ at $\frac ab,\frac cd$ with diameters $\frac1{b^2},\frac1{d^2}$ are in the configuration. Also $ad-bc=a(q-b)-b(p-a)=aq-bp=\pm1$, so by (ii) they are tangent, hence the circle $\Gamma_3$ between them (tangent to both and to the axis) was drawn at some stage. By (i), $\frac1{\sqrt{\delta_3}}=b+d=q$, so $\delta_3=\frac1{q^2}$, and with $XZ:ZY=d:b$ the tangency point is $Z=\frac{bX+dY}{b+d}=\frac{a+c}{b+d}=\frac pq$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-05b.title: Rational tangency points
chmmc-2012-winter-power-05b.body: We show by induction on the order of construction that every circle touches the axis at a rational point and has diameter $\frac1{m^2}$ for a positive integer $m$. The two starting circles do ($0$ and $1$, diameter $1$). If the parents have diameters $\frac1{m_1^2},\frac1{m_2^2}$ and touch the axis at rational $X,Y$, then $\sqrt{\delta_1}:\sqrt{\delta_2}=\frac1{m_1}:\frac1{m_2}$ is rational, so $Z=X+\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}(Y-X)$ is rational, and the new diameter is $\frac1{(m_1+m_2)^2}$. Hence all circles touch the axis at rational points, and none at the irrational $r$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-06.title: Boundary of a region
chmmc-2012-winter-power-06.body: Let $R$ be such a region. A single circle cannot bound $R$, and the only other tangencies are with the $x$-axis, which also cannot bound a bounded region by itself; so the boundary of $R$ contains a point of tangency of two circles $C_1,C_2$, with $C_2$ the smaller. If $C_1,C_2$ are the two starting circles, $R$ is the shaded region of the figure, bounded by these two and the Figure 1 circle. Otherwise $C_2$ was drawn between $C_1$ and an earlier circle $D$, and $C_1,C_2$ are also both tangent to the later circle $D'$ drawn between $C_1$ and $C_2$. On either side of the point of tangency, $R$ is bounded by $C_1,C_2,D$ or by $C_1,C_2,D'$, each a triple of mutually externally tangent circles. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-07a.title: Vertical line
chmmc-2012-winter-power-07a.body: The vertical line $\ell:x=\alpha$ meets the circle tangent at $\frac pq$ (radius $\frac1{2q^2}$) iff $\left|\frac pq-\alpha\right|\le\frac1{2q^2}$. So we count circles that $\ell$ meets. If $\alpha=\frac pq$ is rational, $\ell$ moving up from the axis starts inside the circle at $\alpha$ and leaves it at height $\frac1{q^2}$; above this height it can only meet circles of larger diameter, and there are finitely many of those. If $\alpha$ is irrational, start at $\left(\alpha,\frac12\right)$ inside one of the large circles and move down. Suppose $\ell$ enters only finitely many circles. As it reaches the axis at $(\alpha,0)$ it is either inside a circle, which would be tangent to the axis at $(\alpha,0)$, contradicting irrationality; or inside a region outside the circles, which would touch the axis, contradicting the region property. So $\ell$ meets infinitely many circles, giving infinitely many solutions. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-2012-winter-power-07b.title: Consecutive circles
chmmc-2012-winter-power-07b.body: The vertical line $\ell:x=\alpha$ passes through circles whose diameters $\frac1{q_k^2}$ decrease with $k$, so $\frac{p_k}{q_k}$ is the $k$-th circle $\ell$ enters (moving down). After leaving the circle at $\frac{p_k}{q_k}$, $\ell$ passes through a region outside the circles (bounded by three mutually tangent circles) before entering the circle at $\frac{p_{k+1}}{q_{k+1}}$. Both circles are on the boundary of that region, and any two of the three circles around a region are tangent. Hence they are tangent and $|p_kq_{k+1}-q_kp_{k+1}|=1$. $\blacksquare$
